title: Research methods and reproducibility in the brain and behavioral sciences
stage: Graduate study and research in neuroscience
audience: a graduate preparing for research in neuroscience or cognitive science, or a graduate student in the first years of a PhD or a research role
purpose: Learn how research on the brain and behavior is done well: reading papers, sharpening a research question, design and power, the replication crisis and what caused it, preregistration and registered reports, analysis flexibility and double dipping, open data and code, research ethics with people and animals, writing and presenting, peer review, and research careers, with a realistic picture of the field.
primary_reading: Improving Your Statistical Inferences by Daniël Lakens (free online)

weeks.1: How to read a neuroscience or psychology paper
weeks.2: Finding and sharpening a research question
weeks.4: The replication crisis: evidence and causes
weeks.6: Analysis flexibility, double dipping and circular analysis
weeks.8: Research ethics with people and animals
weeks.9: Writing a paper: structure, figures and claims

blocks.deliverable: Write a one-page summary and critique of a paper.
Compute the power of a supplied published design.
Week 7 midterm; audit a paper with a reproducibility checklist.
Write a referee report on a supplied short paper.
Give a recorded ten-minute talk on a paper.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Registered report: write a stage-one registered report for a study you could run with modest resources, with the introduction, hypotheses, a design with a power analysis, a preregistered analysis plan, the ethics approval you would need, and a data and code sharing plan, then write a referee-style critique of your own proposal.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
